sources.headline: What will Trump’s latest tariffs mean for the world?
sources.text: Inside StoryNew measures come after previous trade tariffs ruled illegal.The United States has issued tariffs of up to 20 percent against 14 major trading partners, including China and the European Union.They replace previous levies struck down by the US Supreme Court.So, why is President Donald Trump coming back with more – and how will China and others respond?Presenter: Rishaad SalamatGuests:Greg Swenson – Founding partner of Brigg Macadam, a banking firm focused on international financing; chairman of Republicans Overseas UKZichen Wang – Deputy secretary-general of the Center for China and Globalization in BeijingMujtaba Rahman – Managing director for Europe at the Eurasia GroupPublished On 26 Nov 2026

sources.headline: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
sources.text: The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy. The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of the country's biggest trading partners - China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions, including Japan, South Korea and Taiwan.The White House began investigating the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal.China is facing the highest tariff rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35%, with others facing either 20% or 25%. The US Trade Representative (USTR) announced the proposed tariffs together with extensive reports of how each jurisdiction's trade practices purportedly impact American commerce.The new duties are not expected to take effect until next year and have to go through rounds of public consultation and, potentially, hearings.Tariffs are taxes levied on imported goods. The amount is typically calculated as a percentage of a good's value and paid to the government by businesses importing products.Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to. Individual countries also face different levies.The proposed tariffs will affect goods from China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India.The USTR's Jamieson Greer said the latest tariffs issued would "level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy".He said that many of America's trading partners had "for decades" adopted industrial strategies which included "targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression". They also employ "other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America's manufacturing base", Greer said.But economists have warned tariffs can fuel inflation and push prices up for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs, as well as dampen global trade.Trump has repeatedly threatened or imposed tariffs during his second term, arguing they will boost US manufacturing and create jobs.Despite a poor result for the Republican party in the midterm elections, the president has continued to press on with his flagship trade policy.Trump is also seeking to cut the US trade deficit - the gap between the value of goods it buys from other countries and those it sells to them.These new levies are build on a "stronger legal foundation" under US law compared with Trump's April 2025 Liberation Day tariffs, Singapore Management University economics lecturer Chang Pao-Li said.Trump previously invoked emergency presidential powers to impose tariffs that have since been struck down, while his latest approach relies on the USTR's authority to impose tariffs to address certain foreign trade practices, she said.The levies are still likely to face legal challenges, but there has been a "historical precedent" for such tariffs remaining in force, Chang said. Many tariffs imposed under Section 301 - a law that allows the US to probe and retaliate against foreign trade practices - during Trump's first term remained in effect during his successor Joe Biden's administration.However, Stephen Brown, chief North America economist for Capital Economics, said the latest tariff announcement was "not as alarming as it looks", due to the taxes "essentially replacing" previously announced tariffs made in the summer."The increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we've been assuming for our forecasts, although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices," he said in a note.The additional tariff burden is likely to be small because a limited number of goods are subject to the new duties, Brown added.Jurisdictions affected by the new wave of tariffs have voiced their disapproval over the Trump administration's move.Washington has also proposed a 10% tariff on goods from Brazil, as part of a separate investigation over what it says are "harmful trade practices" undercutting American workers.Brazilian authorities expressed their "outrage" at the announcement, saying that the move is aimed at pressuring the government to change regulations around issues like digital trade.The South American nation faces duties on finished aircraft and sugar sold to the US."Brazil will not yield to such threats," President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's office said.The European Commission rejected the new US tariffs, saying it would investigate the reasons for bringing them in. It pointed out that tariffs are limited to the 15% previously agreed.The latest tariff rate is "not consistent" with the reality of bilateral economic-trade cooperation between the US and Vietnam, Vietnamese Deputy Prime Minister Bui Thanh Son said.The Japanese government said the US tariffs were "regrettable", while the Singapore government said it disagrees with the White House's findings and that it is engaging the USTR to explore ways to reduce the tariff.South Korea's trade minister said the proposed 15% tariff will be "more than a decent outcome" as it would fall in line with a previously agreed limit with Washington.Last year, Seoul pledged $350bn (£267bn) in US investments in exchange for lower tariffs as part of a trade deal.US trading partners have been "waiting for this shoe to drop" and have argued that they are being wrongly accused of producing too much, said the Asia Society Policy Institute's Wendy Cutler, a former senior US trade negotiator."Many believe that China, not them, should be the target for US action," she added.Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun described the new tariffs as a form of "political manipulation", describing as "false" the US claim that China produces more than it can consume.The tariff announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, who remain locked in a trade dispute and the AI race.The two countries have also been embroiled in a tit-for-tat tariffs war, which is currently on hold.Despite last week's meeting between Trump and China's President Xi Jinping, the two sides made no announcement on the trade war truce, which is set to expire on 10 January.Beijing has remained vague on how it will respond but for now seems "prepared to live with the new rates provided they don't exceed 20%", Cutler said. Additional reporting by Leehyun Choi in Seoul

EU says 'strongly' rejects premise of new US tariffs

Issued on: 25/11/2026 - 20:48
Modified: 25/11/2026 - 20:54

Share

The EU said Wednesday that it rejected the premise of new tariffs on its exports proposed by the United States and expected Washington to stick by a deal struck with Brussels last year. The US unveiled proposed tariffs on 14 economies including the European Union and China, after a months-long probe into alleged excess production. FRANCE 24's Dave Keating reports from Brussels.

sources.headline: US proposes surprise new tariffs on Brazil imports, including 10% duty on aircraft
sources.text: WASHINGTON – The United States proposed adding new tariffs on goods from Brazil on Nov 25, including a 10% duty on finished aircraft, saying Brasilia had failed to rectify what Washington calls “unreasonable” trade practices.The move is part of a broader round of tariffs the Trump administration has announced on goods from more than a dozen trading partners. It caught Brazil off guard just a month after a presidential election in which US tariffs and influence featured heavily.Brazil’s government said Washington’s announcement was unacceptable and aimed to pressure Brazil into changing its regulatory measures.US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said his office was proposing changes to tariffs imposed in July after Brazil made “no meaningful progress” on the issues. The changes would give Washington more leverage to pressure Brazil to drop the practices, he said.Brazil was the first country targeted under US President Donald Trump's new tariff strategy, which relies on Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, an unfair trade practices statute. The US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s previous global tariffs under an emergency law, including duties of up to 50% on Brazilian goods, in February.Under the proposal, finished Brazilian aircraft, which are currently exempt, would face a 10% duty. Aircraft are Brazil’s fourth-largest export to the United States, and the measure could hit plane-maker Embraer hard.The company’s shares were down over 3% on Nov 25 afternoon. The company said in a statement it was reviewing the US government’s announcement, adding that Embraer “continues to believe in and strongly defends maintaining the zero-tariff regime for the global aerospace industry, which has been in place since the 1980s”.Two people at the company, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said the announcement was a surprise.Aerospace has largely escaped the tariffs that have hit other sectors such as autos, steel and aluminum. But tariffs on Embraer commercial jets would pose problems for US airlines, which have no domestic alternative for flying regional routes to smaller cities.New sugar duty proposedWashington is also proposing a new tariff rate on out-of-quota raw and refined sugar that enters the US on a nondiscriminatory basis, the US Trade Representative’s office said. This would ensure that sugar from Brazil could not be shipped through third countries into the United States.The impact may be limited, however. Brazil’s sugar exports to the US have dwindled to just over 146,000 tons in 2026 through the end of October, down from more than 1 million metric tons in 2024, according to industry body UNICA.The US already plans to cut Brazil’s tariff-free raw sugar quota for 2027 by about a third, to 100,000 tons.Renato Cunha, CEO of industry group NovaBio, said the new tariff will not directly affect producers in Brazil’s north and north-east, which benefit from the quota, though he called the tariff “negative” and said it “highlights the unpredictability of these actions interfering in the market”.Greer said the sugar and aircraft duties were meant to bring Brazil to the negotiating table, and that Washington remains open to talks.Washington accuses Brazil of unfair practices on a range of issues from illegal deforestation to Brazil’s instant payment system, Pix, which the US government argues disadvantages credit card companies. Brasilia has rejected all the allegations.Outrage in BrasiliaBrazil’s government expressed its “outrage” at the announcement in a statement on Nov 25 evening, and said the proposed tariffs aimed to pressure Brazil into changing regulations around issues including Pix and digital trade.Brazil and the US established a working group in September to drive negotiations over tariffs and a broader bilateral trade framework after an August call between President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Trump, but Brazilian officials say a proposal from Washington that Brasilia had expected never materialised.“The USTR’s unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the ongoing bilateral negotiation process. Brazil will not yield to such threats,” Lula’s government said.Lula won a new term in late October, defeating right-wing opponent Flavio Bolsonaro, who had campaigned on stronger ties with the Trump administration. During the campaign, Lula described US tariffs on Brazilian goods as election interference meant to benefit his opponent.Brazil asked on Nov 24 for the creation of a dispute panel at the World Trade Organization to examine the July Section 301 tariffs, a move the US blocked the same day.The July tariffs, which followed months of fruitless negotiations between US and Brazilian officials, had maintained and expanded exemptions for Brazilian beef, coffee, aircraft and other goods.Brazil also faces an additional 12.5% tariff under a separate Section 301 investigation into connections to forced labor in the supply chains of dozens of countries.The USTR will hold a hearing on the duties on Jan 14, before they can take effect. REUTERS
